Bannock

Bannock histories connect the Snake River Plain with Northern Paiute communities and wider Great Basin and Rocky Mountain travel networks. At Fort Hall, Bannock and Shoshone people share the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes government while maintaining distinct languages. Community publications connect treaty history, language teaching, food sovereignty, and environmental stewardship.

Names & relationshipsBannock is closely connected to Northern Paiute and shares government with Shoshone people at Fort Hall. Bannock and Shoshoni are linguistically distinct. Sources about the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe shared institutions and should not be presented as evidence of a separate contemporary Bannock-only government.

Start reading here

Bannock people and their Northern Paiute language variety remain distinct from Shoshoni; Fort Hall has a shared Shoshone-Bannock government. The 2020 journal article was previously read in its introduction, Edmo narrative and recording notes; current journal access has not been rechecked. Edmo's 1959 recorded account is one person's mediated history, and treaty metadata discrepancies remain unresolved.

  1. About: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes — culture and history

    The Tribes' Culture and History account introduces Bannock relationships and Fort Hall's shared community without assigning all joint territory exclusively to Bannock people.

  2. Bannock (Fort Hall, Idaho)

    Lizzie Edmo's attributed autobiographical material and recording notes provide a named Fort Hall speaker's perspective within a specialist language study.

  3. Embracing Tennambo’i: The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ Connection to Craters of the Moon

    This Tribal department's guest essay connects ancestral travel, food places, public interpretation and camas stewardship in its own voice.

  4. Shoshone-Bannock Tribes recognize Fort Bridger Treaty Day

    The Tribes' Treaty Day article explains their interpretation of the promised Bannock reservation and later shared Fort Hall history.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

People, language relationships, and homelands

Bannock is both a people’s name and the name of a Northern Paiute language variety. Linguist Tim Thornes locates historical Bannock territory around the Snake River Plain of southwestern Idaho and the Boise River Valley, and describes sustained contact with Shoshoni. The Tribes’ own overview places Bannock bands within a shared history with Northern Shoshone bands, across ancestral lands extending well beyond present reservation boundaries. Their related Numic languages belong to the Uto-Aztecan family. A shared government and close cultural relationships coexist with linguistic distinctions; neither Bannock nor Northern Paiute should be treated as simply another name for Shoshone.

Read the sources [1] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [2] International Journal of American Linguistics / University of Chicago Press

02

Routes, place names, and responsibilities to land

The Language and Cultural Preservation Department’s 2024 essay describes Tennambo’i, the lava-flow country now within Craters of the Moon, through ancestral memory and living place names. It connects routes across the Snake River Plain with salmon fishing, buffalo hunting, and camas and wild-carrot gathering farther afield. These paths linked important food areas and relationships across a large region. The department also explains its work with the National Park Service to bring tribal interpretations into public signage. Its account connects historical travel with present responsibilities, including collaborative efforts against invasive grass threatening camas habitat at Centennial Marsh.

Read the sources [3] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes Language and Cultural Preservation Department / National Park Service

03

The treaty, an unfulfilled reservation promise, and Fort Hall

The treaty signed at Fort Bridger on July 3, 1868, contains different provisions for Eastern Shoshone and Bannock people. Article 2 promises a future Bannock reservation; the published text names Portneuf and “Kansas Prairie,” while the Tribes’ public interpretation identifies Camas Prairie. Article 4 addresses reservation residence and hunting on specified unoccupied lands. In its Treaty Day account, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes explains that the separate Bannock reservation was never created and that Bannock people were instead relocated to Fort Hall in 1869. The Tribes’ historical overview describes subsequent losses through surveying, legislation, and allotment. Reading the treaty beside tribal interpretation helps distinguish the agreement’s text from what the United States actually implemented.

Read the sources [4] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes, reproducing Charles J. Kappler’s treaty compilation [5] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [1] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes

04

Camas, colonial deprivation, and food sovereignty

A 2023 study coauthored by tribal citizens and university researchers connects the Bannock War of 1878 with restricted access to food, damage to camas grounds, and unmet federal obligations. Its historical discussion places hunger and displacement at the center of the conflict rather than describing war as an isolated outbreak. The study also documents a contemporary project to make camas more accessible at Fort Hall through cultivation experiments and community activities. Seeds and transplanted bulbs offered possible ways to strengthen access, although the authors identify questions about genetic differences and longer-term effects. This work connects experimental science, tribal oversight, and relationships maintained through food.

Read the sources [6] Journal of Ethnobiology / SAGE

05

Language teaching and a narrator’s history

The Tribes’ Language and Cultural Preservation Department describes instruction in both Bannock and Shoshone, taught by tribal members and connected to history, identity, and treaty knowledge. Its archival and digital preservation programs retain documents, recordings, interviews, and family histories. Thornes’s 2020 publication provides a different kind of evidence: Bannock-language narratives with transcription, grammatical analysis, and translation. The autobiographical narrative of Lizzie Edmo was recorded by Sven Liljeblad at Fort Hall in 1959. Her recollections describe travel, gathering, fishing, and exchanges among families. The article preserves an individual speaker’s experience and linguistic knowledge; it should not be generalized into a single life story for every Bannock family.

Read the sources [7] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [2] International Journal of American Linguistics / University of Chicago Press

06

Shared government and the care of public history

The published constitution and bylaws identify the Fort Hall Business Council as the governing body of the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes and provide for seven elected members. The document records a constitution approved in 1936 and later amendments. This is a primary source for the shared government’s formal structure, rather than a description of every earlier Bannock political arrangement. Cultural work is also institutional: the preservation department maintains archives, supports historical research, and addresses misleading representations and exploitation of tribal intellectual property. Its museum presents community history, art, and the Benedicte Wrensted photographic collection. Publicly shared information sits alongside material the department explicitly treats as confidential or sensitive.

Read the sources [8] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [7] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes

07

Horses and knowledge passed within families

The Tribes describe Indian relay racing as a continuing horse tradition passed to younger generations by tribal families. Its public explanation outlines a team of four people and three horses, with the rider changing horses between laps while teammates manage the exchanges. This gives readers a concrete view of coordination and skill. The page’s broader claims about the sport’s origin represent the Tribes’ own account; this profile does not turn its undated historical claims into a precise chronology.

Read the sources [9] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes

08

Fish, water, energy, and contemporary priorities

The shared government’s Fish and Wildlife Department links habitat restoration and fisheries work to the exercise of treaty rights. The Tribes’ salmon advocacy also calls for removal of the four lower Snake River dams, framing recovery as a cultural responsibility as well as an ecological issue. Its Water Resources Department describes protection of water quality, administration of reservation water use, and implementation of the 1990 Fort Hall water agreement. A separate 2022 Community Action Plan brings air monitoring, community survey findings, renewable energy, and efficiency measures into environmental planning. Together these sources show distinct forms of contemporary tribal action. They document governmental priorities and proposals, rather than proving that every proposed project or policy has been completed.

Read the sources [10] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [11] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [12] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [13] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes, Tribal Department of Energy

What needs further research

  • Add more Bannock-authored or community-approved family histories and public oral histories, including experiences beyond Fort Hall; one narrator cannot represent every band or family.
  • Deepen the 1878 war account with community interpretation and critically assessed archival records, including differing experiences among Bannock, Northern Paiute, and Shoshone families.
  • Compare the published treaty text with manuscript and official publication records, and document the chronology of Fort Hall boundary changes without collapsing promises, executive orders, and later legislation into one event.
  • Add a dated community account of Bannock language learning and teaching outcomes; no current speaker total is asserted here.
  • Expand evidence on schooling, livelihoods, art, and family life, and verify permissions and cultural suitability before reproducing archival images or knowledge.
